summary: Kole Jain takes a skincare website from Dribbble, critiques it element by element, and redesigns its desktop hero into a split-screen beauty landing page. He removes elements that do not earn their place (social links, a page outline on a short site, a written testimonial in the header, decorative shapes), fixes the layout first, and resizes the design to a real browser viewport of 1920 pixels across by about 1,000 pixels tall instead of the taller canvas Dribbble shots use. He then reworks the nav around a logo placed front and center, turns product photos into a card slider, fixes the hero's contrast by choosing a better photo and adding a subtle overlay, reuses the brand font (Apple's New York) from the logo and packaging, and adds subtext with a primary and a secondary call to action. For a design system, it shows a critique-then-rebuild process for marketing heroes, a realistic viewport check, and the habit of reusing brand typography across logo, packaging and UI. He openly says parts of the result favour looks over usability, so those choices are taste, not rules.
key_ideas: A skincare website should lead with great product photos, a bright white background and lots of white space.
New and interesting layouts are welcome, but like everything in design they can be taken too far.
Critique the existing design element by element before changing anything, keeping what works (the top nav and its icons).
When elements are everywhere with no clear layout, fix the layout first and remove what is not needed.
An ultrawide layout that splits the screen into two halves is common on modern beauty websites.
Design a desktop hero for a real browser viewport: about 1920 by 1,000 pixels, not a tall Dribbble canvas that hides what would be cut off.
Simplify a nav by collapsing secondary links into a menu button, turning the cart into an icon and the profile into 'sign in'.
When there is not enough room to show every product, turn the product cards into a slider.
Fix hero contrast by first choosing a better photo (right vibe, nothing in the way, good lighting), then adding a subtle overlay if it is still a little bright.
Reuse the font already on the logo and packaging for the website heading; he 'may as well use it here too'.
He finishes the hero with subtext plus a primary and a secondary call to action.
Use ready-made product mockups instead of making product renders from scratch.
He finds beauty packaging has too much stuff on it from an aesthetic standpoint; for a minimal look he wants less on the pack.

rules.rule: Design desktop hero sections for a real full-screen browser viewport of 1920 pixels across by about 1,000 pixels tall, not a taller showcase canvas.
rules.why: Most non-curved monitors give only about 1,000 pixels vertically with the browser bar; taller Dribbble-style canvases hide content that would be cut off.

rules.rule: For a skincare or beauty website, lead with great product photos on a bright white background with lots of white space.
rules.why: That is what he thinks a skincare website should look like, and the Dribbble original had none of those things.
rules.evidence: when I think of a skincare website

rules.rule: When elements are scattered with no clear layout, fix the layout first before refining visuals.
rules.why: The original had things everywhere with no clear layout, so layout was the first fix.
rules.evidence: no clear layout so let's fix that first

rules.rule: Try interesting, new layouts instead of boring, repetitive structures, but stop before the page loses a clear layout.
rules.why: He calls boring, repetitive website structures the bane of his existence, but says like all things in design new layouts can be taken too far; the original missed the mark and had things everywhere with no clear layout.
rules.evidence: like all things in design it can be taken too far

rules.rule: Don't put social links in the header of a product landing page [inferred: the exact spot is only shown on screen, next to the top nav].
rules.why: Having social links there doesn't really make sense, so he packs them up.
rules.evidence: having Social Links here doesn't really make sense

rules.rule: Skip an on-page site outline on a short landing page; keep it for pages long enough to warrant it.
rules.why: He says it is not a bad idea, but sites like this typically aren't long enough to warrant it.
rules.evidence: aren't long enough to Warrant it

rules.rule: Don't show social proof as a written testimonial in the header.
rules.why: Social proof is good, but not in that form in the header; he removes it from the hero.
rules.evidence: not in the form of a written testimonial in the header

rules.rule: Don't keep decorative shapes that aren't helping the design.
rules.why: The original's shapes (which he says look like the character from Google Dino Run) weren't helping out, so he removes them.
rules.evidence: get rid of the Dino Run shapes too those aren't helping out

rules.rule: Give the hero a larger image without cutouts.
rules.why: He says the original image isn't bad, but it would be nicer if it felt larger and didn't have the cutouts.
rules.evidence: it'd be nice feels larger and didn't have these cutouts

rules.rule: For a modern beauty website hero, consider an ultrawide split layout: image and text in the left half, product images in the right half.
rules.why: Splitting the screen into two halves is pretty common on modern beauty websites.
rules.evidence: split the screen into two halves

rules.rule: When the logo goes front and center in the nav, collapse secondary links (favorites, notifications) into a menu button, show the cart as just an icon and turn the profile link into 'sign in'.
rules.why: The original came without a logo, so he puts one front and center and slims the other nav items around it [inferred: he gives no reason for each change].
rules.evidence: collapse favorites and notifications into a menu button

rules.rule: When there isn't room to show every product card, make the cards a slider.
rules.why: He wanted to display all the products but didn't have a ton of room.
rules.evidence: we're going to make this into a slider

rules.rule: When a hero photo hurts contrast, first choose a better photo (right vibe, nothing in the way, good lighting), then add a pretty subtle overlay if it is still a little bright.
rules.why: He needed to address the contrast; photos failed when they weren't the vibe, things were in the way or the lighting was way off, and the one he picked was still a little bright. The contrast problem is with the hero text on the photo [inferred].
rules.evidence: we need to address the contrast here

rules.rule: Reuse the font already used for the logo and packaging for the website's hero heading.
rules.why: New York was already used for the logo and on the packaging, so he 'may as well use it here too'.
rules.evidence: we've used it for the logo and on our packaging

rules.rule: Give the hero heading supporting subtext plus a primary and a secondary call to action.
rules.why: He adds them as the last pieces of the hero; he states no rule or reason.
rules.evidence: some subtext and a primary and secondary call to action

rules.rule: Use ready-made product mockups to show a real-looking product instead of building renders from scratch.
rules.why: The page needs an actual product that looks good, and he does not make it from scratch.
rules.evidence: found a few matching mockups on minimal mock ups.com

decisions.question: What canvas size should a desktop landing page hero be designed at?

options.name: Tall showcase canvas
options.effect: Fits much more content in one shot, but a large part would be cut off on a real screen.
options.when: Showcase shots only; he calls it a trick most Dribbble designers use to include way more.

options.name: Real browser viewport (1920 by about 1,000 pixels)
options.effect: The hero is squished to what people actually see above the fold on a full-screen browser.
options.when: Whenever the design should match reality.

decisions.recommendation: Real browser viewport: 1920 pixels across but only about 1,000 pixels vertically on most monitors with the browser bar.

decisions.question: How should a beauty or skincare landing page hero be laid out?

options.name: Free-form experimental layout
options.effect: Interesting and new, but taken too far it leaves things everywhere with no clear layout.
options.when: Only with restraint; he likes new layouts but warns they can go too far.

options.name: Ultrawide two-half split
options.effect: Image and text on the left half, product images on the right half; a clear, familiar structure.
options.when: Modern beauty websites, where it is pretty common.

decisions.recommendation: The ultrawide two-half split, because it is common on modern beauty websites and fixes the lack of a clear layout.
decisions.evidence: an ultrawide layout where we split the screen into two halves

decisions.question: How do you fix contrast when the hero text sits on a photo? [inferred: text on the photo]

options.name: Choose a different photo
options.effect: A photo with the right vibe, nothing in the way and good lighting gives the text room.
options.when: First, when the image fights the text.

options.name: Add a subtle overlay
options.effect: Dims a photo that is still a little bright so text stands out.
options.when: After choosing the photo, if it is still too bright.

decisions.recommendation: Do both in order: find a better image, then add a pretty subtle overlay if it is still bright.
decisions.evidence: we need to address the contrast here

options.name: Written testimonial in the header
options.effect: Clutters the hero; he removes it.

process.detail: Go element by element: keep what works (top nav, fitting icons) and note what doesn't (social links, site outline, cut-out image, header testimonial, decorative shapes, copy like free shipping over $500).
Find matching product mockups (minimalmockups.com) and use Photoshop to make the product look good; make a logo and packaging, looking at real packaging (L'Oreal) and aiming for minimal and bougie.
Remove unneeded elements (social links, testimonial, site outline, decorative shapes) and pick a clear structure: an ultrawide two-half split with image and text on the left, products on the right.
Squish the design to 1920 pixels across by about 1,000 pixels tall to match a full-screen browser on most monitors.
Put the logo front and center, collapse favorites and notifications into a menu button, make the cart an icon, turn profile into 'sign in', and add a search bar for balance.
Build a product card (decide which corners hold the buttons), turn the cards into a slider and add a 'new arrivals' chip.
Search for a hero image with the right vibe, no clutter and good lighting; add a subtle overlay if it is still bright.
Use the logo and packaging font (New York) for the hero heading.

process.step: Add copy and calls to action
process.detail: Add subtext, a primary and a secondary call to action, and (for looks) an arrow-only button that leads to the full product line.

examples.visual_note: Top nav with icons, social links, a page outline, an image with cutouts, a written testimonial in the header, decorative shapes he says look like the Google Dino Run character and a 'free shipping over $500' line; things everywhere with no clear layout.

examples.visual_note: The 1920 by about 1,000 pixel dimensions of a full-screen browser laid next to the Dribbble design, showing that a whole part of the shot would be cut off entirely.

Ultrawide two-half layout: hero image with a subtle overlay, New York heading, subtext and primary plus secondary calls to action on the left; product card slider with a 'new arrivals' chip on the right [inferred: he first moves the product images to the right]; logo front and center, menu button, cart icon, 'sign in' and a search bar in the nav; an arrow-only button added for looks.
Card with the product mockup and buttons placed in chosen corners, used in a slider.

Minimal packaging in the New York font with a line borrowed from a super blurry reference photo, contrasted with busy L'Oreal packaging. One element was centered, so the one below could not also be centered; moving it to the side left too much empty space. He changed the color and made many small tweaks over about 5 hours.

caveats: He says he keeps 'the lack of ux' so the redesign stays Dribbble-worthy, favouring aesthetics over usability; the search bar ('regardless of if it's really needed') and the arrow-only button ('it just looks good') are taste, not usability advice.
The 1920 by about 1,000 pixel viewport is his observation from his own monitor and 'most other monitors', not measured data; it covers desktop only.
Self-promotion in the description: a free Figma file on his site, a minimalmockups.com link, and a Newform design community challenge with $1500.
Auto-captions: the invented brand name is unclear ('delis'), the logo line reads 'let's get our T SM front and center', and 'this font also pass the go' likely means the original font had to go.
Short, informal video (5 minutes 41 seconds, March 2025); it is one redesign of one Dribbble shot, so its layout choices are specific to beauty and skincare sites.
